{
  "title": "Cruz and Phoenix and the Brick That Glowed",
  "subtitle": "The night a gray LEGO brick took them all the way to Billund",
  "chapters": [
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 1: The Warm Gray Brick",
      "text": "Cruz was building a LEGO shark on the bedroom floor, way past bedtime, and Phoenix was making his dinosaur ROAR at the shark's pointy fin.

"Sharks are scarier," said Cruz.

"Dinosaurs are BIGGER," said Phoenix, and roared again just to prove it.

Digging through the bottom of the LEGO bin, Cruz found one plain gray brick. It felt warm, like it had been sitting in the sun. Phoenix poked it with one finger.

The brick began to glow gold. It went **BZZZT**, and hummed like a tiny bee.

"Cruz," whispered Phoenix, "is it awake?"

Cruz pressed it. **WHOOOOSH!** The bedroom carpet spun away like water going down a drain, and the boys landed with a soft *thump* on a wooden floor covered in curly wood shavings.",
      "shout_line": null
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 2: The Duck With Wheels",
      "text": "A man in an apron was carving a little wooden duck, and the duck had wheels instead of feet.

"Well now," the man said, smiling. "Visitors." He held up the duck. "I'm **Ole Kirk Christiansen**, and I make toys, right here in **Billund, Denmark**. Started back in **1932**."

Phoenix gasped. "A duck that ROLLS?"

"People didn't have much spare money back then, for new tables or chairs," Ole Kirk explained, "so I made toys instead, to keep families smiling."

Cruz looked closely at the duck's wheels. They wobbled a little. "They'll roll smoother if you sand this edge," he said, and rubbed the wood with his sleeve until it was silky smooth.

Ole Kirk rolled the duck across the workbench. It glided like it was skating.

"Only the best is good enough," Ole Kirk said, pointing to a sign on the wall with those very words carved into it. "That's my motto, and now, thanks to you, it's true of this duck too."",
      "shout_line": null
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 3: Play Well",
      "text": "Two years later — the humming brick zipped them ahead, **WHOOOOSH** — Ole Kirk stood on a stool with a fresh sign.

"I need a name for the company," he said. "Something that means what we're doing here."

"What about the ducks?" asked Phoenix.

Ole Kirk laughed. "Close! I've mixed two Danish words together: ***leg godt***." He tapped the sign. "It means **'play well.'** And it's **1934**, so that's official now."

Phoenix stood up on the workbench stool, arms out wide.

"PLAY WELL!" he shouted, and everyone in the workshop shouted it right back.",
      "shout_line": "PLAY WELL!"
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 4: The Fire and the Rebuild",
      "text": "Smoke curled under the workshop door. **CRACKLE, CRACKLE.**

"Oh no," said Cruz, as everyone hurried outside. The workshop had caught fire in **1942**, but every single person got out safely — Ole Kirk made sure of that.

The next morning, the workshop was just ashes and beams. Ole Kirk stared at it with his hands on his hips.

"Build it bigger!" Cruz said, grabbing a fallen beam to carry it clear. "You did it once, you can do it again — even better!"

Ole Kirk's face broke into a grin. "You know, young man, I think you're right."

So they built. Hammers banged, boards went up, and by the end of the chapter — with a little bit of glowing-brick magic to speed things along — the new workshop stood taller than before.",
      "shout_line": null
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 5: Bricks That Wouldn't Hold",
      "text": "Years later, the workshop had a brand-new machine that squeezed hot plastic into little bricks called **Automatic Binding Bricks**, sold starting in **1949**.

Phoenix stacked five of them into a tiny tower for his dinosaur to guard.

**Ker-CLUNK.** The tower wobbled.

**SPLAT.** It fell right over, and the dinosaur went tumbling with it.

"These bricks are SLIPPERY," Phoenix announced, hands on his hips, sounding very much like a dinosaur expert giving a serious opinion.

A worker nearby sighed. "He's right. They just don't grip."

Cruz picked up one of the fallen bricks and turned it over in his fingers, thinking hard about how his own LEGO shark set clicked together so well back home.

"Somebody needs to fix the underneath," he said.",
      "shout_line": null
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 6: The Tubes",
      "text": "A man with a notebook came striding over — Ole Kirk's son, **Godtfred Kirk Christiansen**.

"Fix the underneath, you say?" Godtfred crouched down next to Cruz. "I've been thinking the very same thing. Every set should connect to every other set. That's the whole idea of a system."

Cruz flipped a brick over and pointed into the hollow underneath. "What if there was something in here to grab onto the bumps on the brick below?"

Godtfred's eyes lit up. He sketched little round **tubes** inside the bottom of the brick, right there in his notebook.

They pressed two new bricks together.

**CLICK!**

Phoenix grabbed the tower, turned it upside down, and shook it as hard as his arms could manage.

It held.

"IT CLICKS!" Phoenix shrieked, and Cruz cheered right along with him. The new brick was patented on **January 28, 1958** — and it's the very same brick still used today.",
      "shout_line": "IT CLICKS!"
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 7: The Boy Who Tested Toys",
      "text": "A small boy about Cruz's size was crouched on the floor, snapping bricks into a wobbly tower and testing whether it would fall.

"I'm **Kjeld**," he said. "Godtfred's my father. My job is to test every new toy before anyone else gets to play with it."

"That's the BEST job," said Cruz.

Kjeld grew up to run the whole company. In **1968**, Billund opened an entire park built from millions of bricks, called **LEGOLAND** — and by **1978**, tiny yellow-faced people called **minifigures**, with bendy arms and legs, had joined the bricks on every shelf.

Phoenix found a minifigure and gave it a paper dinosaur hat he folded himself. Cruz built it a little brick shark to ride.

"Only the best is good enough," Cruz said, and the minifigure, riding its shark, seemed to agree completely.",
      "shout_line": null
    },
    {
      "heading": "Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet",
      "text": "**WHOOOOSH.** The bright Billund workshop spun away, and the boys landed softly back on their own bedroom carpet.

Cruz's LEGO shark was right where he'd left it. Phoenix's dinosaur was still roaring silently on the rug. And there in Cruz's palm sat the little gray brick, glowing gently now instead of humming, like it was tired and happy.

"Same brick," Cruz whispered, clicking it onto the shark's fin. It fit perfectly, of course — bricks always do.

Phoenix yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn and flopped onto his pillow.

"Play well," he mumbled.

"Play well," Cruz whispered back, and set the glowing brick gently on the windowsill, ready for next time.",
      "shout_line": null
    }
  ],
  "ending_line": "Goodnight, Cruz. Goodnight, Phoenix. Play well.",
  "true_facts": [
    {"text": "LEGO began in **Billund, Denmark**, with a carpenter named **Ole Kirk Christiansen**, who started making wooden toys in **1932**.", "fact_id": "f1"},
    {"text": "The name comes from the Danish words ***leg godt***, meaning **'play well,'** chosen in **1934**.", "fact_id": "f2"},
    {"text": "One of the first wooden toys was a pull-along **wooden duck on wheels**.", "fact_id": "f3"},
    {"text": "Ole Kirk started making toys because families in the **1930s** had no spare money for new furniture.", "fact_id": "f4"},
    {"text": "The workshop burned down in **1942**, and everyone got out safely — Ole Kirk rebuilt it bigger than before.", "fact_id": "f5"},
    {"text": "Ole Kirk's motto, **'only the best is good enough,'** was carved on a sign in the workshop.", "fact_id": "f6"},
    {"text": "The first plastic bricks, sold from **1949**, were called **Automatic Binding Bricks**, and they didn't hold together well.", "fact_id": "f8"},
    {"text": "Ole Kirk's son **Godtfred** realized toys needed a system, so every set could connect to every other set.", "fact_id": "f9"},
    {"text": "The fix was **hollow tubes** inside the underside of the brick, gripping the studs of the brick below.", "fact_id": "f10"},
    {"text": "The modern LEGO brick was patented on **January 28, 1958**, and those old bricks still fit bricks made today.", "fact_id": "f11"},
    {"text": "**Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen**, Godtfred's son, tested toys as a boy and later ran the whole company.", "fact_id": "f12"},
    {"text": "**LEGOLAND** opened in Billund in **1968**, built from millions of bricks.", "fact_id": "f13"},
    {"text": "The **LEGO minifigure**, with its yellow face and bendy legs, arrived in **1978**.", "fact_id": "f14"}
  ],

It opens a whooshing doorway into a real moment from history, then carries the boys home again and waits, glowing gently, on the windowsill for next time."}
    ],
    "ending_summary": "Cruz and Phoenix returned from 1930s-to-1970s Billund with the Glow Brick clicked onto Cruz's LEGO shark, and set the still-glowing brick on the windowsill ready for their next adventure."
  },
